en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 23, the Vammikasutta (The Ant-hill Sutta) [The Buddha said: "Suppose, bhikkhus, there were an ant-hill here that was ancient, long-standing, and had been built up over time. And suppose a man would come along with a shovel and a basket, intending to remove the ant-hill. He would dig around it on all sides with his shovel, and as he dug, he would throw away the earth in his basket. Thus, by repeatedly digging around it with his shovel and throwing away the earth in his basket, he would eventually make that ant-hill level with the ground, having completely removed it. So too, bhikkhus, a noble disciple considers this: 'This body of mine has form, is composed of the four great elements, produced by mother and father, built up from rice and gruel, subject to impermanence, to being worn and rubbed away, to dissolution and disintegration. And this consciousness of mine is supported by it and bound up with it.

When he dwells thus contemplating the body as body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world, then the mind becomes concentrated within, calm, unified, and one-pointed. Just as when a skilled turner or his apprentice, when making a long turn, knows: 'I am making a long turn,' or when making a short turn, knows: 'I am making a short turn'; so too, when a noble disciple dwells thus contemplating the body as body... the mind becomes concentrated within, calm, unified, and one-pointed. This is called a noble disciple who dwells in the first stage of enlightenment, having become certain of the path, having transcended doubt, and having gained confidence in the Dhamma. "Furthermore, bhikkhus, suppose a man comes along carrying a torch against the wind. What do you think, bhikkhus? Would that man’s torch go forward?"—"No, venerable sir."—"So too, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these five aggregates subject to clinging, then he is called a noble disciple who dwells in the second stage of enlightenment... "Furthermore, bhikkhus, suppose a cowherd were to drive cattle across a fordable river. As he drives them across, he would see the footprints of those cattle that had crossed before. What do you think, bhikkhus? Would that cowherd drive those cattle back again to the near shore?"—"No, venerable sir."—"So too, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these five aggregates subject to clinging, then he is called a noble disciple who dwells in the third stage of enlightenment... "Furthermore, bhikkhus, suppose a cowherd were to drive cattle to a pasture rich in grass, water, and shelter. What do you think, bhikkhus? Would those cattle live happily and grow strong?"—"Yes, venerable sir."—"So too, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these five aggregates subject to clinging, then he is called a noble disciple who dwells in the fourth stage of enlightenment, one who has reached the stream, not subject to perdition, firmly established, destined for full enlightenment. "Bhikkhus, just as an ant-hill might be seen rising out of a forest thicket, and a man would come along with a shovel and a basket, intending to remove the ant-hill; and as he dug around it with his shovel and threw away the earth in his basket, he would eventually make that ant-hill level with the ground, having completely removed it; so too, bhikkhus, a noble disciple considers this: 'This body of mine has form... and this consciousness of mine is supported by it and bound up with it. When he dwells thus contemplating the body as body... the mind becomes concentrated within, calm, unified, and one-pointed. This is called a noble disciple who dwells in the first stage of enlightenment... [as above]. "Furthermore, bhikkhus, suppose a man comes along carrying a torch against the wind... [as above]. "Furthermore, bhikkhus, suppose a cowherd were to drive cattle across a fordable river... [as above]. "Furthermore, bhikkhus, suppose a cowherd were to drive cattle to a pasture rich in grass, water, and shelter... [as above]. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Kumārakassapa was dwelling in the Blind Men’s Grove.
Then a certain deity, of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Blind Men’s Grove, approached.
Having illuminated [the area], she approached the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa; having approached, she stood to one side.
Standing to one side, that deity said this to the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa:
"Monk, monk, this anthill smokes by night and blazes by day."
The brahmin spoke thus:
“O wise one, take up the knife and dig.
Digging repeatedly and taking up the knife, the wise one saw a plowshare.
“O cripple, venerable sir,” the brahmin said,
“lift up the cripple!”
“Scratch, O wise one, taking up the knife.
Scratching and taking up the knife, the wise one saw a swelling.
“A swelling, venerable sir,” he said.
The brahmin spoke thus:
“Throw away the swelling corpse;
take up the sword, O wise one, and dig!”
Searching repeatedly, the wise one took up his sword and saw a forked path.
“A forked path, venerable sir,” the brahmin said.
Thus spoke the brahmin.
"Throw open the forked path;
dig with the sword, O wise one!
Digging with the sword, the wise one saw the crossroads.
“‘A water-strainer, venerable sir,’ he said.
The brahmin spoke thus:
‘Throw away the water-strainer.’”
“Scratch, O wise one, taking up the knife.
Scratching while taking up the knife, the wise one saw a tortoise.
“A tortoise, venerable sir,” he said.
The brahmin spoke thus:
“Lift up the tortoise;
strike with the sword, O wise one.”
Searching with wisdom, he took up his knife and saw a butcher’s block.
“A butcher’s block, venerable sir,” the brahmin said.
Thus spoke the brahmin.
"Throw away the butcher's block;
take up the knife and cut, O wise one.
Cutting away and taking up the knife, the wise one saw a lump of flesh.
‘A piece of meat, venerable sir,’ he replied.
The brahmin said this:
‘Throw away the piece of meat.’
"Scratch, O wise one, taking up the knife.
As the wise one scratched, taking up the knife, he saw a nāga.
"It is a nāga, venerable sir," he said.
The brahmin spoke thus:
“Let the Nāga be; do not disturb the Nāga; pay homage to the Nāga.
“Monk, you should approach the Blessed One and ask him about these questions; and you should remember them exactly as the Blessed One explains them to you.”
“Bhikkhu, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins,
its devas and humans, who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions,
other than a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from such a person.”
This is what that deity said.
Having said this, she vanished right there.
Then, at the end of that night, the Venerable Kumārakassapa approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the Venerable Kumārakassapa said this to the Blessed One:
"Bhante, last night, when the night was far advanced, a certain deity of surpassing beauty approached the entire extent of [this place]..."
Having illuminated the blind grove, he approached me and stood to one side.
Standing there to one side, venerable sir, that deity said this to me:
“Monk, monk! This anthill smokes by night and blazes by day.”
The brahmin spoke thus:
“O wise one, constantly take up the sword.
Constantly taking up the sword, O wise one... [and so on].
"Or having heard it from here.
This, venerable sir, is what that deity said.
Having said this, she vanished right there.
"Venerable sir, what is the anthill? What is the smoking at night? What is the blazing by day?
Who is the brahmin? Who is the wise one? What is the weapon? What is the constant gnawing? What is the creeper? What is the swelling?
What is the forked path? What is the sieve? Who is the tortoise? What is the butcher’s block? What is the piece of meat? Who is the elephant?"

“‘Ant-hill,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for this body composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, fed on rice and gruel, subject to impermanence, to being rubbed and massaged, to breaking apart and disintegration.
Whatever one reflects upon and ponders at night concerning one’s work by day—
this is the ‘smoking’ at night.”
“Bhikkhu, whatever work one undertakes by body, speech, or mind during the day after having reflected and deliberated throughout the night—
this is the burning during the day.
‘Brahmin,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
“‘Sumedha,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for a bhikkhu in training.
‘A knife,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for noble wisdom.
‘Carving away,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for the arousal of energy.”
“‘Lame one’ (laṅgī), bhikkhu, is a designation for ignorance.
‘Throw out the lame one, abandon ignorance;
sharpen the knife, O wise one,’ this is its meaning.”
“‘Bloating,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for anger and resentment.
‘Cast out the bloated one; abandon anger and resentment;
sharpen the sword, O wise one’—this is the meaning of it.”
"Bifurcated path," bhikkhu, is a designation for doubt.
"Cast off the bifurcated path, abandon doubt;
constantly wield the sword, O wise one"—this is its meaning.
“‘A trap-door,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for the five hindrances, namely:
the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.
Throw open the trap-door; abandon the five hindrances.”
"Constantly, O wise one, taking up the sword"—this is its meaning.
"The tortoise," bhikkhu, is a designation for the five aggregates of clinging, namely:

the aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, the aggregate of clinging to perception, the aggregate of clinging to volitional formations, and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness.
"Throw out the tortoise; abandon the five aggregates of clinging;
strike repeatedly, O wise one, taking up the sword"—this is its meaning.
"The butcher's knife and block," bhikkhu, is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure.
Of forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire,
and provocative of lust; of sounds cognizable by the ear … [and so on] … of odors cognizable by the nose … [and so on] …
Toward tastes cognizable by the tongue … and toward tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust.
Lift up the butcher’s knife; abandon the five strands of sensual pleasure.
"O wise one, constantly taking up the sword"—this is its meaning.
"A piece of meat," bhikkhu, is a designation for delight-and-lust (*nandīrāga*).
"Throw away the piece of meat; abandon delight-and-lust."
“‘O wise one, constantly taking up the sword’—this is its meaning.
‘Nāga,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed.
‘Let the Nāga stand; do not provoke the Nāga; pay homage to the Nāga’—this is its meaning.”
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
The Venerable Kumāra Kassapa was satisfied and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The third discourse, the Vammikasutta, is finished.
